title: Looking back: the long hymns
hook: Sukhmani, Asa di Var, Barah Maha and the ninth Guru's saloks

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the daily banis, Jaap at dawn to Sohila at night, and your line, the day, held. Which edge of your day got a line? Today, the long hymns. Day six hundred ninety-three.

Some prayers fit in a breath. Others take an hour and more, and people make room for them anyway. In many Sikh homes, when someone is ill or a family is starting something new, relatives gather on the floor to read Sukhmani Sahib together, start to finish, passing the reading along. In gurdwaras before sunrise, ragis are already singing a ballad that will run until the sky goes pale. Long hymns ask for something short ones don't: time, and often company. This year gave you four of them. Looking back: the long hymns.
screen: `SOME PRAYERS FIT IN A BREATH.` → `SOME TAKE AN HOUR, TOGETHER.` → `FOUR LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: First, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's psalm of peace, in Raga Gauri. Twenty-four ashtpadis, each opening with a salok and then eight stanzas. Read straight through, it takes around ninety minutes; many read one ashtpadi a day. Its refrain names the whole hymn: sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam, the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name, the resting place of the devotees' minds. We spent a hundred days on it, longer than on anything else this year. Second, Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's ballad for dawn. A var was a hero's ballad, the kind sung about kings and battles. Guru Nanak took the form and turned it inward: twenty-four pauris, with saloks of Guru Nanak and Guru Angad, and in the gurdwara Guru Ram Das's chhants sung between them. Its first salok is gratitude: balihaaree gur aapne, a sacrifice to my Guru, a hundred times a day. Third, the Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's twelve months in Raga Majh. In the old Punjabi form, a woman longs for her absent beloved as the seasons turn; here the longing is the soul's, for God. It opens with people separated by their own deeds, asking in mercy to be united, and it's read in many gurdwaras on Sangrand, the first of each month. Fourth, the saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, near the very end of the Granth. Short, calm couplets about a world that passes and a Name that stays. One says the wise person frightens no one and fears no one. Four long hymns, four moods: peace, gratitude, longing, steadiness. And this week held its own long hymn of days: the Gurus' gurpurabs, the first installation, the Granth made Guru, and the daily banis.
screen: `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `ASA DI VAR: A BALLAD AT DAWN.` · `BARAH MAHA: TWELVE MONTHS OF LONGING.` · `THE NINTH GURU'S STEADY SALOKS.` · then, large: `THE LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one favorite. Peace, gratitude, longing or steadiness: pick the one you need today. Find a few lines of it in a gutka, a gurbani app, or simply in memory, and read them slowly, twice. Don't try to finish anything. Then sit with what you read for the rest of the time, letting one phrase come back now and then, like a tune you can't shake. If you pray, you can let those lines carry your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Four long hymns side by side: Sukhmani's peace, Asa di Var's gratitude, the Barah Maha's longing, and the ninth Guru's steady saloks.
Your line: the long hymns. Today, give one thing more time than it strictly needs: a meal, a phone call, a page. Day six hundred ninety-three. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily or in family gatherings, gurdwaras sing Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha is read on Sangrand, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of a full reading of the Granth.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak. a var is a ballad sung about kings and battles. what do you do with the form?
options: use it for the inner life and praise of God.
write a ballad about a famous battle.
fork.reveal: Asa di Var keeps the ballad's shape, twenty-four pauris, but its battles are inward, and it opens in gratitude to the Guru.

original.note: Punjabi: the jewel of peace, the name of Guru Arjan's long hymn in Raga Gauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: long hymns are for experts with hours to spare.
what it means: Sikhs read them a little a day, or together, so the length is shared.

what a scholar hears: both Sukhmani's twenty-four ashtpadis and Asa di Var's twenty-four pauris are numbered structures, and tradition holds that the ninth Guru's saloks were added when the Granth was completed at Damdama.
